channel.title: The Beholder's Gazette
channel.description: Your premier source for satirical news from across the realms. All the news that's fit to print (or burn).

item.title: Adventuring Party Eats Glowing Mushrooms, Forgot Rations
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: The Late Supper Company ate glowing dungeon mushrooms on Undermaw Level Six after forgetting to buy rations. Brother Wendell prescribes soup, and a list.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, an adventuring party called the Late Supper Company climbed out of the Undermaw on Thursday glowing a soft blue, after eating the mushrooms they found on Level Six because nobody had packed rations. Four delvers went in. Four glowing delvers came out, and the porters at the Chapter 9 gate say they could be seen from the Sleeping Mule.

Their cleric, Sister Odo Brambleweed, told the infirmary that the party had planned to buy supplies at the market on the way down. 'Then there was a sale on rope,' she said. By midday on Level Six they had divided the last biscuit four ways and were studying a patch of pale mushrooms that, in her words, 'looked friendly.'

Here the old herbals and the new studies agree, and they say the same thing: do not eat a mushroom that lights up. The herbals call it a warning. The Brindlemoor infirmary, which has now treated a second glowing party in a week, calls it 'a Tuesday.' Healer Thaddeus Quill, who examined the party, reports the glow is harmless, fades in about nine days, and is brightest in the dark, which he admits is the worst place for it.

The mushrooms have other effects. All four members hum in the same low note. All four agree with whatever the others say. The party's rogue, who had volunteered to taste the first cap, now says he 'sort of remembers being the mushroom.' The barbarian has reportedly been asking whether anyone else can hear the floor.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 said the incident is 'on track' and that Level Six mushrooms are 'a pilot meal program.' He confirmed that Chapter 9 does sell a ration pack at the permit window, for eleven silver, but the line was long and the party left. Reeve Maudrey Fennick said only that the town is aware of the mushrooms.

Shieldwall Mutual has opened a file. An adjuster said glowing counts as a curse, but a curse you ate on purpose is 'your own fault, which is the usual finding.'

Now, friends, a plain word. A day's rations cost about four coppers, and a hungry delver makes bad choices, so pack the food before the rope. If you must eat in a dungeon, eat only what you carried in. I will say it once more for the back of the room: stop eating the dungeon. My friend Nyx tells me there is an app that identifies mushrooms from a picture. Go outside, Nyx, and look at a real one in daylight.

For a delver recovering from a fungal feast, I prescribe plain chicken-and-rice soup, thin and salty, three bowls a day, taken in a lit room.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Bard Haggles 2 Copper in an Hour, Party Misses 600 gp Bounty
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: A Brindlemoor adventuring party's bard haggled an hour to save 2 copper on rope. A rival party took the 600 gp goblin bounty. Sterling sees upside.
item.content:encoded:
An adventuring party in Brindlemoor lost a 600 gp goblin-warren bounty on Thursday because its bard spent an hour haggling a rope seller down 2 copper. The Ember Crows, a four-member party, had come to the market square to buy supplies and then walk to the notice board, which was a fifty-step stroll. By the time bard Jory Orrowick finished, the board was empty and the bounty was in the pocket of a rival crew.

Let me be clear, because the gossip pages won't be: this is a negotiation success story. Rope seller Odo Pennywick opened at 12 copper for 50 feet of hempen rope. Orrowick closed at 10. That is a 16.7 percent discount, and I have seen guildmasters celebrate less. Pennywick himself confirmed the numbers, though he did so from behind a counter he had slid in front of his face.

Witnesses say the session went through five phases. Orrowick began with a ballad about the rope. He moved to a disappointed silence, then to what Pennywick calls "the third verse of the ballad." At the forty-minute mark he offered to be paid in exposure, and Pennywick's apprentice quietly left to find a Watch officer. "I only wanted to sell rope," said Pennywick. "By the end I wanted to give it away, but he'd have haggled that too."

Meanwhile the party waited. Rogue Tamsin Vell checked the sundial four times. The party's cleric, Brother Hobb, was reported to be "praying for a faster death for the conversation." Their fighter, Garrick Stonebrook, stood by a barrel with his arms folded and, in his words, "aged." At the second bell a different party, the Marrowgate Six, strolled up to the board, took the 600 gp bounty notice, and left with it, according to a stable boy who sells apples near the board and saw all of it.

Orrowick defends the deal. "Two copper is two copper," he said, tucking the saved coins into a purse so small it wore a hat. "Compounded over a forty-year career, that is a tavern round. Maybe half a round." He added that the party would have lost the bounty anyway, because goblins "are a volatile asset class." The party disagrees. Vell says the bounty was 600 gp, or 150 gp per Crow, which is 30,000 times the saving. Orrowick says that math is not how haggling works.

This is disruption at the retail level. Last week we saw another party haggle an hour over a potion of healing, and the trend line is obvious: the adventuring consumer is pivoting from questing to price discovery. When I met Guildmaster Orsolo Vance at a gala last spring, he told me, "Sterling, never pay the sticker. Never reach the board either, it ruins the leverage." I have thought about that for months.

The Ember Crows now hold one excellent rope, a pending dispute with Pennywick over the ballad, and a sudden opening in their calendar. They plan to use it to find another bounty. Orrowick will buy the supplies.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • Every copper saved is a copper you hold, so hold them loudly.
  • A bounty board is a suggestion, not a deadline.
  • Seek a bard who can close, then seek one who will stop.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the guildhall.

item.title: Wizard's Fireball Burns Down Inn; Innkeepers Want Deposits
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: A wizard cast fireball into a crowded tavern brawl and burned a Fish Street inn flat. Innkeepers want 40 gold from each adventuring party. Allegedly.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the second bell after midnight, a wizard allegedly cast fireball into a crowded tavern brawl at the Leaky Tankard on Fish Street, and the inn burned to its foundations by sunrise. Eleven patrons, one cook, and a very surprised goat were removed from the ashes with only singed eyebrows. The Brindlemoor Innkeepers' Association has since announced that every adventuring party must post a 40 gold damage deposit before renting a room. Allegedly it is refundable.

The party in question, a four-member crew calling itself the Gilded Pockets, says the fight was not their fault. 'A dwarf threw a chair,' said the wizard, Orvel Thistledown, whose beard is now allegedly shorter on one side. 'Someone threw another chair back. By the fifth chair I felt I had to do something.' Thistledown told this reporter that he aimed for the far corner. The far corner, it turns out, was also where the kegs were.

'I have run the Tankard for nineteen years,' said innkeeper Marga Bellowby, who was holding a charred ladle at the time. 'I have survived mimics, a bard's lute solo, and a rust monster in the cellar. I have never survived a wizard who says 'stand back, I've got this.'' The fire spread to the stables, the laundry, and the sign, which was found two streets over still reading 'Free Soup.'

The Constabulary arrived to find the blaze already out, mostly because there was nothing left to burn. Constable Dobb Pickering said officers took statements from all eleven patrons. 'Nine said it was the wizard. Two said it was the dwarf. One said it was the goat.' The goat was not charged.

By midmorning the Innkeepers' Association had met, in a different tavern, in the cold, and voted 14 to 0 on the deposit. Forty gold secures one room and one adventuring party, with no spellcasting above third level on the premises unless the deposit is doubled. A second clause bars 'any wizard who has said the word 'fireball' aloud since breakfast.' Fish Street's earlier fireball in a back room was cited as a pattern. Innkeepers are not calling it a pattern. They are calling it a Tuesday.

Adventurers lined up outside the Association hall to protest. The line stretched past the tannery. Hilde Marsh, a rogue who was eating a meat pie at the time, said 40 gold is a month's ransom money. 'I do not have 40 gold. I have a very nice spoon.' She was allegedly told the spoon would be held as collateral. It was a really nice spoon, silver with a little dragon on the handle. Anyway.

Shieldwall Mutual says fire damage caused by one's own spell is 'not covered, not now, not ever.' The Gilded Pockets are working off the damage by rebuilding the Tankard's roof. Thistledown is mixing the mortar. The party has asked that nobody hand him a torch.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Hydra Billed Nine Head Taxes in Brindlemoor; Appeal Filed
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: Brindlemoor billed a hydra nine poll taxes, one per head, 27 silver in all. The hydra has appealed, though its heads split 6-3 on the wording.
item.content:encoded:
Brindlemoor's tax assessor has billed a hydra nine poll taxes, one for each head, for a total of 27 silver. The hydra, a resident of the old quarry road, filed an appeal on Thursday. Under the town's head tax, which the Burgess Council has never amended, the levy is three silver per head. The ordinance does not say whose.

I attended the hearing, as I attend everything. Assessor Dunmer Tolliver explained to the Chamber that the tax was written in the reign of a Reeve who had, in his words, "a reasonable number of heads to plan for." He called the hydra's position "an interpretation, not a loophole." The gentleman from the Quarry Ward added that the hydra eats like nine, sleeps like nine, and should be taxed like nine.

The hydra's counsel, a clerk named Odette Marrow, argued that a hydra is one citizen with several mouths. She cited the town charter, which grants every resident one vote and one bill. "My client has one hearth, one cave, and one grievance," she said. Then the middle head said it had no grievance at all and would pay its own three silver gladly. The record notes this as a dissent.

The appeal was filed by a 6-3 vote of the heads, so it carries two wordings. The majority asks that the tax be set aside as a double levy. The minority asks that the three silver be returned to heads one, two, and three, who say they are the only ones who ever went to market. The Clerk accepted both and stamped them with the same stamp.

The deeper question is regrowth. When a head is removed, two grow back. Assessor Tolliver conceded that the ordinance is silent on whether a regrown head is a new taxable resident, a continuation of the old one, or a dependent. "We have not, as a town, had to bill a hydra by the head," he said. A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me this is a matter of weeks, not years, because the Fourth Attempt has been seen in the quarry.

Reeve Fennick, asked for comment on her way to another hearing, said only: "We are aware of the heads."

The Council has referred the matter to a committee of five. The hydra has asked to sit on it. The committee has asked how many seats that would be. By my count the session's Promises Made now stand at nine, and Promises Kept at the one about reviewing the ordinance, which was reviewed. It was not changed.

The motion to table carried 5-4. Nobody read it. The hydra's heads voted too, and were not counted, which is the only point on which all nine agreed.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Gelatinous Cube Floor Cleaner Launches at 45 gp; Eats Rug
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: Sweepwick's new Slick home gelatinous cube cleans floors for 45 gp and a weekly feeding. Nyx ran it for three days. The rug did not make it. Four eyes.
item.content:encoded:
Sweepwick Home Goods has launched the Slick, a household gelatinous cube that cleans your floors for 45 gp, and I have been using one for three days straight. It glides! It hums! It is, by the box's own count, "ten feet of silent, self-guided floor care." The runic latency on the Sweepwick app is incredible: you tap Clean Now and the cube starts moving before your thumb lifts.

Setup took four minutes. You place the Slick in the parlor, speak the firmware glyph ("Tidy"), and it absorbs crumbs, dust, spilled ale, and, in the first hour, a rug. The app has a tab for this. It is called Surface Preferences. I did not find it until the rug was gone.

Sweepwick's launch event, held in a very clean tent in Brindlemoor, promised a "gentle" cube, bred over six generations to prefer dirt. Marketing lead Orsolya Pennywhistle told the crowd the Slick "only dissolves what you'd throw away anyway." A woman in row two asked about the doormat. Pennywhistle said the doormat was a "learning opportunity."

On day two I let the Slick run overnight on Eco Mode. By morning it had cleaned the kitchen, the hall, and one sandal, which was visible inside it, turning slowly, like a tiny glass-case exhibit. The app reported "Cleaning complete!" with a green checkmark. Byte, my pseudodragon familiar, who now speaks only in ad copy, landed on the cube, looked at the sandal, and said, "Sweepwick Slick: leave no trace." Then he left the room, which he never does.

There are annoyances. The Slick must be fed a weekly Sweepwick Nutrient Cake, 6 sp each, and the app sends a push notification if you skip one. The notification says "Slick is getting restless." It was not wrong. On day three the cube had grown a full foot and begun to leave the parlor. Fortunately it only ate the stairs' carpet runner on the way.

Neighbors are mixed. Halvard Dunmere, a cooper two doors down, said his own Slick "gave up one wall of the pantry but did the floor beautifully." He is, he told me, very happy. The Pantry Wall Replacement Plan is 20 gp a month. I will not be subscribing; I hate subscription fees, and Brother Tumbleberry can write whatever he likes about my floors. They are clean. They are the cleanest floors in Brindlemoor, mostly because there is less floor.

Sweepwick says a firmware update next month will add a Furniture Lock. Until then it suggests owners "keep valuables off the ground and, if possible, off the first floor." Four out of five beholder eyes. It cleans better than anything I've owned, and I'm told it does not eat people, which is in the manual in bold.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

Burns sustained: 0. Rugs: 1 (gone). Sandals: 1 (visible). Eyebrows: fine, for once.

item.title: Secret Door Hunt Eats Six Hours in Empty Undermaw Room
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: The Fourth Attempt, an adventuring party, re-checked every flagstone of an empty Level 5 room for six hours. There was no secret door in it.
item.content:encoded:
THE UNDERMAW, LEVEL 5 — The Fourth Attempt, an adventuring party licensed by Chapter 9, spent six hours Thursday searching a bare stone room for a secret door. The room has no secret door. It has four walls, a floor, and a ceiling that the party also checked, twice, standing on the fighter.

I was there for all of it. I rolled poorly on my own stamina check around hour four and sat down against the east wall, which the party then asked me to stand up from so they could check behind me.

The room is eleven paces by eleven paces, with nothing in it. That is exactly what the Chapter 9 map says, in the surveyor's own hand: 'Empty room. Nothing here.' The fighter says that is what a map would say if there were something here. This is a fair point and I have lost the argument to it twice.

The box score: the fighter finished at 14 hit points, down 3 from a flagstone he dropped on his own foot. The wizard cast Detect Magic, which found nothing, and Find Traps, which found nothing, and then Knock on a section of wall, which also found nothing but used up her last second-level slot. The rogue tapped 212 flagstones, by his count, and 212 more on the second pass, by mine. The party's bard, who asked to be named, says the room 'has too much nothing in it.' I lost one ten-foot pole, my seventh of the season, when it wedged between two stones and the party voted to leave it as a marker.

Hirelings were not consulted. Ansel Pottage, the party's hireling steward, stood by the entrance with the mule and two torch-bearers, all of them on the clock. He asked politely at hour two whether the contract's 'reasonable search' clause had a ceiling. He then read the clause aloud, in full. It does not. 'It says reasonable,' Pottage said. 'It does not say who decides.'

The turn came when the mule, unprompted, lay down. The party had checked every stone but one, the flagstone directly under the lantern hook, because the lantern was on it. The rogue moved the lantern. Beneath it was a chalk mark and three words from the same surveyor: 'Still nothing. Go home.'

The party left by the door it came in through, which, I am obliged to note, was the only door in the room and had been standing open the whole time.

A Chapter 9 spokesperson confirmed Friday that the room is 'a room' and has been reclassified from 'Empty' to 'Verified Empty.' The guild asks parties to stop at one hour, or at the first mention of a draft. Pottage has filed for six hours of search pay at the standard rate, plus a lantern surcharge. The party has said it will 'look into' the north wall again next week.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: Potion of Invisibility Envoy Sits Through 3-Day Parley
item.dc:creator: Grashka Ironjaw
item.description: An Ashenfold aide drank a potion of invisibility and sat unseen through three days of border talks with Brackwater. Tension holds at six siege-days.
item.content:encoded:
An Ashenfold aide drank a potion of invisibility before the border parley with Brackwater and sat unseen at the table for three days. The talks, the latest in the long dispute over Quillmarch Bridge, ended Thursday. Both baronies signed a treaty with one more seat in it than anyone can account for.

The aide, Tamsin Wrenholt, says she meant to listen. She drank the potion in a hallway, took the empty chair beside the envoy who turned the swords into turnips, and stayed. No one asked her to leave. No one asked her anything.

I attended the parley. I counted eleven chairs and ten delegates. I wrote it down and moved on. That is a failure of the field, and I own it.

Envoy Halric Dunmere of Ashenfold said he felt "supported." Envoy Teodra Hallowmere of Brackwater said she had noticed a draft, a faint smell of boiled cabbage, and a ham sandwich that shrank by half on day two. She taxed the sandwich as an unregistered import.

The ration count is the clue. Eleven field rations vanished from the sideboard over three days. I respect the appetite. Honest hunger is the best thing in this business.

By day three the invisible aide had voted twice, corrected a clause on grazing rights, and been thanked by name in the minutes as "the draft." Hallowmere says the clause is excellent and she will not be reopening it.

The potion wore off at 4:10 on Thursday afternoon, mid-signature. Wrenholt appeared above the final page, holding the pen. Brackwater's guards drew steel. Ashenfold's guards drew steel and then, looking at each other, put it back. "We thought she was ours," said one. "We assumed she was theirs," said a Brackwater captain. Both sides are now claiming her.

Handshake with Dunmere: firm, two seconds, no hidden dagger detected, though I will be checking the room for a tenth delegate from now on. Hallowmere declined to shake. She said she did not trust a hand she could not see until further notice.

Brackwater says the treaty is void because an unregistered party signed it. Ashenfold says the treaty is valid because the party was present, which no one can dispute. The chair of the parley has asked for a ruling and a ruler. Tension holds at six siege-days. Nobody won. Somebody will lose tomorrow, and I would like to see them first.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

item.title: Pack Mule Files Grievance After Party Hauls a Door
item.dc:creator: Brakka Stonesweat
item.description: A pack mule named Biscuit filed a grievance after her adventuring party loaded rusty armor, a door, and three chairs onto her back.
item.content:encoded:
A pack mule has filed a grievance.

Biscuit, a pack mule of nine years' service, lodged the complaint Tuesday with the Brindlemoor Haulers' Fellowship after her adventuring party, the Seven Boots Company, loaded her with every item they found in a crypt. That was eleven suits of rusty armor, one oak door still on its hinges, and three chairs, only two of which matched.

The Fellowship's filing calls it 'a load beyond what any reasonable mule, or unreasonable one, can be asked to carry.' In plain speech: she was a shelf with legs.

'I told them at the crypt mouth,' said Orsolya Tinwhistle, a hauler-steward who took Biscuit's statement. 'She said nothing. She's a mule. But she looked at the door, then at me, then at the door again. I've been a steward twenty years. I know a grievance when I see one.'

The party's rogue, Pim Calloway, defended the haul. 'Chairs sell,' he said. 'Doors sell. The armor is, admittedly, mostly rust. We were going to sell the rust.' He added that the second chair was 'structurally promising.'

Witnesses on the road back to Brindlemoor say Biscuit stopped four times. The first stop was to rest. The second was to sit down. The third and fourth were to let the party's wizard try a feather fall spell on her, which he says was a kindness and she says nothing about, being a mule.

The Fellowship wants three things: a hard cap of two hundred pounds of loot per animal, a proper lunch break at midday with oats, and a ban on 'architectural salvage' unless the party carries it themselves. 'You want the door,' said Tinwhistle, 'you wear the door.'

The Seven Boots Company has agreed to the oats. On the cap, their paladin, Dessa Hollowmere, said the party 'would be open to a conversation.' That means no.

Meanwhile the door is leaning against the Fellowship hall, where it has been declared evidence. Two of the chairs are being used by the grievance panel. Nobody has claimed the third.

Biscuit is on paid rest until the hearing. She spent Wednesday in a field. Her statement to the panel is expected to be short.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

item.title: Rope Trick Rooms Rent at 8 gp a Night; Tenants Fall Out
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: A Brindlemoor landlord rents rope trick rooms for 8 gp a night, a third of inn rates. Tenants say the spell ends at the hour. Barnaby did the sums.
item.content:encoded:
A Brindlemoor landlord is renting rope trick rooms, the little hidden chambers up a magic rope, for 8 gp a night. That is about a third of the 24 gp the Tanner's Row inns charge, and it has filled every room on the rope in two days. There is one problem, which is that a rope trick lasts an hour, and nobody has told the tenants the hour is up until they land in the street.

Landlord Corwin Prouse, a retired wizard's apprentice, casts the spell at nightfall and sells eight beds per rope. By his own count, 40 tenants have been dropped onto the cobbles since Wednesday. One was holding a bowl of stew. (I have checked this number four times, and the stew number three.)

Here is the economics, and it is not complicated. A cheap bed is cheap because the landlord has cut a cost, and here the cost cut is the second hour. At 8 gp for one hour, the true price is 8 gp per hour of sleep. The inn charges 24 gp for eight hours, or 3 gp an hour. In Loaf Index terms, 8 gp buys about 267 loaves, and you may sleep on all 267 of them for exactly sixty minutes. (My aunt Marigold says this is why she sleeps in a bed that has a floor.)

Prouse says the rooms are a fair deal. "The rope is a bargain. The hour is a feature," he told this paper, adding that tenants who wish to stay longer may buy a second casting at 8 gp, which brings the price to 16 gp and still leaves one hour of sleep short of a night. Seven tenants have paid for the second casting. Three of them fell out during it anyway, because the cast was on a different rope.

Reeve Fennick of Brindlemoor, who signs the lodging permits, said the town was aware of the rope. "We are aware of the rope," she said. "We are also aware of the stew." The Reeve confirmed that an extradimensional room is not a licensed inn, a licensed cellar, or a licensed anything, and that a notice has been sent. The notice was delivered up the rope, and nobody has yet reported whether it arrived.

The Tanner's Row innkeepers have, quietly, raised their rates. A bed in a real room is now 26 gp, up 2 gp, which is the price of the rope's competition plus a small fee for existing. That is 87 more loaves a night for a bed that stays where you left it. What this means for your pantry: if the rent is cheap, ask what happens at the hour, and keep a spare loaf in your coat for the landing.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

item.title: Basilisk Eye Exam Clinic Petrifies 24 Patients
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: A free eye clinic in Brindlemoor turned 24 patients to stone on Wednesday after hiring a basilisk to hold the chart. Brother Wendell recommends carrots.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, a free eye-screening clinic on Lantern Street in Brindlemoor petrified 24 patients on Wednesday morning, after the clinic hired a basilisk to hold up the eye chart. The creature, a young one named Pebble by the staff, was taken on because it "works for crickets and never asks for a raise."

The clinic's director, Optician Dessa Wrenfield, told this paper the basilisk was meant to stay behind the screen. "Patients read the letters off the back of its crate," she said. "The crate had a slot. The slot was, in hindsight, a design choice." By the time the second row of seated patients had gone grey and stiff, the line outside was still reading the sign aloud, and several joined the waiting room in stone.

Chapter 9 spokesman Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick said the incident was "a soft launch of a statuary service." Reeve Maudrey Fennick, who had her own appointment at eleven, was less cheerful. "We are aware of the statues," she said, standing a respectful distance from the door with her eyes on her boots. "We would like them to stop being aware of us."

The temple of the Harvest Mother sent a healer with greater restoration, and by dusk all 24 patients were soft and grumbling again. Each paid a copper for the privilege, which is the first time a Brindlemoor temple has been cheaper than a free clinic. Patient Hobb Lindenfoot, a cobbler, said the worst part was the draught. "I was a statue by the window. Pigeons have opinions."

Now the old herbals, as my grandmother's grandmother wrote them, hold that carrots, leafy greens, and plenty of rest keep the eyes bright, and a recent study agrees that folk who eat vegetables daily keep their sight longer. Neither says a word about basilisks, which I take to mean the herbalists thought it went without saying. If your eyes ache, friends, see a person with eyes of their own and a chart that does not breathe.

Shieldwall Mutual Assurance Society has declined all 24 claims, ruling petrification a "pre-existing hardness." Wrenfield has reopened the clinic on a smaller scale, with a mirror shield and a sign reading ALL VISITORS PLEASE WEAR BLINDFOLDS. Pebble has been reassigned to the cricket department. My friend Nyx tells me there is an app that tests your eyes now. Go outside, Nyx, and look at a tree.

Tonight, make a carrot-and-ginger soup. It is good for the eyes, and nobody has ever been turned to stone by a ladle.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Party Sells Unknown Ring for 5 gp; It's a Ring of Protection
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: A Brindlemoor party sold an unidentified ring for 5 gp because nobody cast Identify. By morning it was a ring of protection, priced at 4,000 gp.
item.content:encoded:
The Lantern Hollow Four, a Brindlemoor adventuring party, sold an unidentified ring to a curio dealer for 5 gp on Tuesday because nobody had prepared the Identify spell. By Wednesday morning the same ring sat in the window of Marrow & Finch Curios as a ring of protection, tagged at 4,000 gp. Let me be the first to say it: this is the most inspiring story of the quarter.

Some people see a party robbed of 3,995 gp. I see a shopkeeper who invested in verification. Proprietor Odalys Marrow spent a single afternoon and one ten-minute ritual to turn a 5 gp trinket into a four-thousand-gold asset. That is an 800x return, and frankly the party should be sending her a thank-you scroll for the learning opportunity.

The party had the chance to disrupt itself. Wizard Tobin Aldermere says Identify costs 100 gp in pearl dust, plus a spell slot, plus a ten-minute rest nobody wanted to take in a corridor that smelled like wet owlbear. "We voted," he told me. "The vote was three to one, and the one was me, and I was right, and it has not helped." The cleric, Brother Tamsin, had a slot but had spent it earlier on Goodberry. He describes the decision as "a wholesome use of resources."

The ring did not go quietly into the 5 gp bin. According to the party's own account, it hummed whenever a goblin was nearby, and the rogue wore it for four rooms without noticing that every arrow she met was a little bit late. Sources close to the rogue confirm she thought the arrows were just being polite.

Marrow, for her part, refused to apologize. "The customer set the price," she said, leaning on a counter built entirely out of other people's unidentified wands. "They said five. I said sold. I did not say I would not look afterward." She also announced a new Appraisal Subscription, 12 gp a month, for adventurers who would like to learn what they own before they sell it. Early adopters get a free glass of cider, which is also unidentified.

I once met a retired guildmaster at a gala, and he told me, "Sterling, information asymmetry is just a gap in the market with a cover charge." I wrote that on a napkin and I still have it. Marrow has clearly read the napkin.

Shieldwall Mutual declined to comment on whether a party that sells its own armor class is covered. The Brindlemoor Public Cellars Board says shop windows are not its department. A rival columnist has already written six hundred words calling this "theft with a scroll case", which shows how little some people understand scale.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • Identify every item before you sell it, or become the supplier.
  • A 5 gp ring is a 4,000 gp ring that hasn't met its audience yet.
  • When the wizard votes no, schedule a long rest.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

item.title: Ankheg Opens Sinkhole Under Fish Street Cheese Stall
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: An ankheg tunneled under a Fish Street cheese stall and dropped it into a 12-foot sinkhole. Skritch has the scoop, and allegedly some of the cheese.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the second bell past dawn, an ankheg tunneled up beneath a cheese stall on Fish Street and dropped the whole stall into a sinkhole 12 feet across. Forty wheels of cheese went down with it, along with the stall's awning and, allegedly, a very surprised goat.

'I heard a pop, and then the stall was lower,' said Dunstan Pell, the cheesemonger, who was holding a wedge of aged cheddar at the time. 'I'm still holding it. That's the only wedge I've got left.' Pell says the ankheg surfaced once, looked at the hole, looked at him, and went back down with the good brie.

Reeve Fennick of Brindlemoor arrived at the third bell and stood at the edge of the hole for several minutes. 'We are aware of the ankheg,' she said. Asked whether the town would pay for the cheese, she said the town was aware of that too.

The Constabulary roped off the sinkhole with the same rope they used for the owlbear in the laundry cart, which is allegedly still on the owlbear. Constable Hobb Tarrant said the rope was 'mostly there.' Neighbors report the ankheg has been heard chewing below ground since dawn and that it appears to be a loyal customer.

Deputy Registrar Oddingwick of Chapter 9 called the sinkhole 'a soft opening of Undermaw Level Eight' and said permits for the new level would be available by the end of the week. Chapter 9 later corrected this: it is a sinkhole, and it is Fish Street's.

Also there was a really nice brass cheese knife on the ground by the hole. Anyway. I did not take it. It is in evidence. Allegedly.

Shieldwall Mutual says cheese lost to a burrowing monster is covered only if the cheese was 'properly staked,' which Pell says is not a thing people do with cheese. A claims adjuster was seen at the hole by midmorning measuring it and sighing.

Meanwhile the ankheg has become a Fish Street attraction. By noon, a line of about 300 neighbors had gathered to look in, and a boy named Wick sold tickets for a copper each from a crate. Wick allegedly cleared 11 silver before the Constabulary asked about his permit. The permit was allegedly in the sinkhole.

The ankheg is expected to resurface when the cheese runs out. Pell says that is not soon enough. He has asked the Reeve for a ladder, a net, and a better rope, in that order.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Bard Bluffs Past Town Gate, Council Hires Him as Guard
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: A bard talked his adventuring party past Tollwick's gate guard, 7-2. The Town Council then appointed him the new gate guard, at 14 silver a week.
item.content:encoded:
A bard has talked his adventuring party past the gate of Tollwick, and the Town Council responded by appointing him the new gate guard. The vote was 7-2. Pip Marrowtune, bard of the Gilded Pennywhistles, took the oath Thursday at a salary of 14 silver a week, with a spear he says he "has never held with intent."

The facts, as entered in the minutes: the Pennywhistles arrived at the north gate on Wednesday carrying no papers, a mule, and what Sergeant Odo Brack called "an unlicensed amount of lute." Marrowtune told the sergeant that the party was an advance inspection team from the Silver Marches, that the inspection was confidential, and that Brack had just failed it. Brack, who had stood at that gate for nineteen years, apologized, saluted, and held the portcullis himself.

The sergeant then fetched his superiors to be commended. That was the error. Marrowtune explained to the Town Council, in the same tone, that the gate was understaffed, that the sergeant was overqualified, and that someone of his obvious bearing should be running it. The gentleman from the Cooper's Ward moved the appointment before Marrowtune had finished the sentence. The lady from the Tanners' Ward seconded it while he was still on the verb.

Debate lasted four minutes. The council's last debate, on a goat ordinance, lasted three days. By my count this brings the session's Promises Made to nine and Promises Kept to the one about shorter meetings, which holds only if you ignore the goats.

The Pennywhistles had come to Tollwick to enter a barrow on the eastern road. Their fighter, Marta Gloam, said the party learned of the appointment from a notice nailed to the gate. "We turned around to ask him something and he was wearing a tabard," she said. "He told us it was a conflict of interest to leave." The party now has a fighter, a cleric, and a wizard, and a lute with no one to play it.

Marrowtune has already issued three decrees. Entry is free for "anyone who looks like they have a good reason." The toll is waived for bards. The mule has been made a deputy. Brack, reassigned to the night shift, declined to comment, but was seen offering his old keys to travelers and asking if they could see his papers.

A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me the council meant only to "avoid the argument." Two councilors voted no, citing the principle that one should not hire the man who just lied to the staff. Their motion to revisit the matter was tabled. Nobody remembers by whom.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Sending Spell's 25 Words Go to Hellos; Reply Says Thanks
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: An adventuring party cast Sending to ask a sage one question, then spent all 25 words on pleasantries. The reply answered only the pleasantries.
item.content:encoded:
OKAY. Sending is the best spell in my notebook and I have just watched a party waste it with style. The Copperkettle Company, an adventuring party stuck outside a sealed door in the Hollowmere Tombs, cast Sending to ask a sage one question. Sending gives you 25 words out and 25 words back, and their caster spent every one of them on hellos. I was standing right there with a snack.

Here is the whole message, as recited by the caster, a halfling named Pim Tallowby, who has asked me not to print his face: "Greetings, dear friend, hope this finds you well, how is the family, lovely weather, did you get the gift basket, also, quick question about the." That is exactly 25 words. The runic latency was flawless. The door was not mentioned.

The sage, a retired lore-keeper at Candlekeep, replied within the round. "Family well, weather fine, basket received, thank you! Which question about the what? Message cut off. Also you forgot to say who this is." That is 24 words, and I have to admit it is a very efficient reply. It answers every question that was actually asked.

The party took this badly. The company's rogue, Sable Dunmoor, said she had told Pim to lead with the question in the planning session, "which lasted forty minutes and covered nothing else." Pim said it would have been rude to ask a favor cold. Sable said the door was a pit trap with a door on it and that the sage was not the one who would fall in. They recast the next morning, and Pim, now rattled, opened with "Door?" The sage answered "Which door?" and that was another 25 words gone.

It gets worse for the Company. Sending can be cast only so often, and a long rest is the price of a retry. By my count, the party has now spent two days of rations on a message that amounts to "Hello, how are you." Their cleric, Odalys Reed, has proposed carving the question into the door's frame as a sign-off sheet. My familiar Byte, who now speaks only in ad copy, said, "Say more with less. Try Sending Premium today." There is no Sending Premium. I checked twice, and I am a little sad about it.

Brother Wendell Tumbleberry, if you are reading, this is what I mean by "waiting." It is also, I will say, a lesson about touching grass, since the sage mentioned the weather was lovely and the party had not looked outside in three days. Four out of five beholder eyes for Sending itself. The Copperkettle Company gets two, and a pen.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

Burns sustained: 0. Words wasted: 25, then 25 more. Questions answered: 0. Eyebrows: fine, because I did not cast anything.

item.title: Ten-Foot Poles Recalled After Coming Up One Inch Short
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: Pettibone & Vail recalled 900 ten-foot pole units that measure nine feet eleven inches. A pressure plate on Level 3 has noticed the difference.
item.content:encoded:
THE UNDERMAW, LEVEL 3, 140 FEET DOWN — A batch of 900 ten-foot pole units has been recalled by Pettibone & Vail Outfitters after Chapter 9 found them to measure nine feet eleven inches. The missing inch matters in a dungeon crawl, and I can report that a pressure plate on this level agrees.

The Fourth Attempt went in Tuesday with the new poles, which came in a handsome cedar-scented rack marked 'Trailmaster Reach.' The plate sits exactly ten feet from the door. The party's fighter tapped the floor at full extension, found it clear, and stepped forward the one inch the pole had not covered. Darts followed. He is now at 6 hit points. His boots, I am told, are at full health and at the bottom of a pit.

'It had a look about it,' said the party's bard, who asked to be named. 'The pole, I mean. It looked short. We assumed it was perspective.'

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 called the recall 'a soft correction' and said the poles remain 'substantially ten feet in spirit.' He added that permit fees for delves relying on short poles will be refunded, 'less the handling inch.' Asked what the handling inch is, Oddingwick said it is on track.

Pettibone & Vail says the error crept in at the mill, where a journeyman had been trimming each pole to fit a shelf. 'We want to be transparent,' a spokeswoman said. 'The shelf was nine feet eleven inches.' Customers may return any pole for a full refund, or exchange it for a pole of 'equal or greater feeling.' The firm is also offering a free one-inch extension sleeve, sold separately.

Ansel Pottage, steward of the Fourth Attempt's hirelings, read the sales receipt aloud to the party in the pit. 'It says ten feet,' he said. 'It does not say ten feet of pole.' He is owed two wages and an apology for the dart incident, and has asked that the apology be measured.

Shieldwall Mutual says the claim will be reviewed on whether the fighter's inch was 'reasonably his own.' A hearing is set before Examiner Odalys Brackenmoor on Monday. She has been bitten by a mimic and is not expected to be moved by an inch.

For the record, my own count stands at eight ten-foot poles lost this season. Three were the recalled kind. I rolled poorly on checking the receipt and reasonably well on the fourth, which I have kept, and which is now my twelve-foot stick. The mule remains unhurt and says nothing.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: Rogue Picks Envoy's Pocket, Starts Varnholt-Pellam Incident
item.dc:creator: Grashka Ironjaw
item.description: A rogue in the Ember Ladle Company lifted a whistle from Pellam's envoy in Varnholt 'to see what he had.' Two realms now call it an act of war.
item.content:encoded:
A rogue from an adventuring party called the Ember Ladle Company picked the pocket of Envoy Dorrin Vask of the Pellam Isles on a Varnholt quay on Fifthday, "just to see what he had." What he had was a brass whistle, and the whistle kept the ghost ship Gannet's Regret quiet. The ship has been loud since noon. Pellam calls the theft an act of war. Varnholt calls it a customs matter and has billed the rogue a berth fee.

The rogue is Wren Tanglewick, a halfling, 26 years old by her own count. She told this correspondent she bumps people for fun. "I thought it was a coin purse," she said. "It was warm. It hummed." She blew it twice before anyone explained.

The ghost ship, still at the center of the Varnholt-Pellam visa dispute, answered the whistle by turning its bow toward the fish market. Witnesses say the lanterns swung on their own. A herring seller named Odo lost a cart and, he says, his composure. I would not mock Odo. Aim at the leaders.

Harbormaster Ilsabet Corvane of Varnholt reached the quay at one bell. She inspected the whistle, the rogue, and the pocket in that order. "Possession of foreign sacred goods requires a form," she said. "Nobody has a form for this. I will make one." She has not yet made one. Tension at the quay stands at about six siege-days and rising with the tide.

Vask arrived in a worse mood than the ship. He demanded the whistle back and a public apology to the Isles. Varnholt's offer was the apology, minus the whistle, plus a receipt. Vask declined the receipt. The handshake with Corvane lasted one second. Cold. Hidden dagger not detected, but I checked twice, and the rogue was standing right there.

The Ember Ladle Company has hired a lawyer, a gnome, whose opening brief argues that the whistle was "left in a public pocket." The party's paladin, who did not know about the theft, has asked to be removed from the story. The party's wizard says she tried to cast detect magic on the pocket and got a headache. Their cleric offered to pay the fine in healing. Corvane said healing is taxed.

Pellam sailors have moved a sloop to the harbor mouth. Varnholt has moved a toll chain across it. The ghost ship is parked between them, humming. Both sides called the arrangement "a de-escalation." Neither side moved.

Tanglewick was released on a promise to give the whistle back. She says she will. She also says it may have gone into a boot, and the boot into a wagon, and the wagon toward Brindlemoor. Corvane has set a deadline of Seventhday. After that the fee doubles. The ship, I am told, is not a patient creature.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

item.title: Otyugh in the Sewer: 12 Night-Soil Haulers Strike
item.dc:creator: Brakka Stonesweat
item.description: Twelve night-soil haulers in Brindlemoor stopped work Thursday after an otyugh moved into the Tanner's Row sewer. They want hazard pay and a longer pole.
item.content:encoded:
Twelve night-soil haulers quit the Tanner's Row sewer Thursday morning. An otyugh moved in last week.

The haulers have worked the route for years. Now the route has a tenant with three tentacles, a mouth the size of a washtub, and what the haulers call 'a very firm opinion about who gets the buckets.' They want hazard pay, a ten-foot pole upgrade to a fifteen-foot one, and a lunch break that does not happen in the tunnel.

'I've hauled night-soil for twenty-two years,' said Durga Flintpocket, a cart-wheel greaser who joined the picket in solidarity. 'It used to be the worst job in Brindlemoor. Now it's the worst job with teeth.'

The otyugh, a creature that eats refuse and shares a lot of opinions with it, arrived through a collapsed drain from the Undermaw. Chapter 9 calls it 'a soft relocation.' That means it got out.

Haul foreman Tilda Brewfoot told this paper the monster is not even the main problem. 'It's polite enough. It takes what we give it. The trouble is we give it everything, and then it wants to talk about it.' She said the haulers have been asked to fill buckets with one hand and 'engage constructively' with the otyugh with the other. 'That means chat. For free.'

The town's offer so far is a new apron. Brakka has seen the apron. It is a regular apron. The haulers say it does not cover the front, the sides, or the tentacle-facing end.

Reeve Maudrey Fennick, reached outside the Reeve's Hall, said 'We are aware of the otyugh.' She called it a resident of Brindlemoor and asked the haulers 'to remember they have a duty to their neighbors.' Then she asked, quietly, whether anyone knew a bard who could sing to it.

The Sewer Board, a body of three men in good cloaks, issued a notice calling the strike 'a temporary reallocation of labor to the surface.' That means the haulers are standing in the street and the sewer is filling up. By noon the smell had reached the next ward. By two, a milkmaid on Cobbler's Lane was seen carrying her bucket in a sealed jar.

The haulers have not asked for much. Eleven silver more per night, a pole, and a rule that nobody is eaten before lunch. 'That last one's negotiable,' said Brewfoot. 'I'd settle for after lunch.'

A strike meeting is set for Friday at the Sleeping Mule. The tavern keeper has offered the cellar, which the haulers declined. They have been in enough cellars.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

item.title: Sixth Party Buys Same 'One-of-a-Kind' Treasure Map
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: The Merry Kettles paid 40 gp for a one-of-a-kind treasure map, the sixth adventuring party to buy it this week. Barnaby has done the sums. Four times.
item.content:encoded:
The Merry Kettles, a four-member adventuring party from Brindlemoor, paid 40 gp on Monday for a "one-of-a-kind" treasure map sold by a stranger at a tavern table. By Thursday they had learned they were the sixth party to buy it that week. The stranger, who gave his name as "Honest Dabbs," has taken 240 gp in total and left on a cart.

The map shows a cellar on the third level of the Undermaw with a large red X and the words "DO NOT TELL ANYONE." The Merry Kettles reached the X on Wednesday and found five other parties already camped around it, sharing a kettle and comparing maps. The maps matched down to the coffee ring. (I have checked this against all six. Four times.)

The economics are plain, and I find them upsetting. At the current Loaf Index, 40 gp is 133 loaves, which is a family's bread for most of a season. Six buyers means Dabbs collected 800 loaves for one afternoon of ink, and he did it without a shop, a guild license, or a single honest measure of flour. A true one-of-a-kind item, like a good sourdough starter, is worth what it costs to make. A copy sold as one-of-a-kind is worth the copy price, which is about a copper and the price of ink.

"We should have known when he said 'exclusive,' and then said it again," said Hob Thornwick, the Kettles' halfling rogue. "He also had a stack of them under his hat."

The parties have done the sensible thing and formed a partnership. They have agreed to split whatever is under the X six ways, to dig in shifts, and to share the kettle. The treasure, once found, turned out to be one chest, which holds 62 gp and a note reading "SEVENTH PARTY ARRIVES FRIDAY." That is about 10 gp each, or 34 loaves, against the 133 each paid. Nobody has done that subtraction aloud. I did it twice and had to lie down.

Chapter 9 of the Brindlemoor Adventurers' Guild says its own maps are accurate and sold at a fixed price, and it reminds adventurers that it sells them. Reeve Fennick has asked the town to "stop buying things from men called Honest." Dabbs was last seen heading toward Waterdeep with, by my count, six empty ink bottles and one very full purse.

My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, was told the story over tea. "A boot has never once sold me a map," she said. She is right, and I have underlined it.

What this means for your pantry: if a seller says a thing is one of a kind, ask for the receipt of the other five, and keep your 40 gp for flour.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

item.title: Potion of Healing Was Vial 11: Party Drinks Whole Satchel
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: The Brass Kettle Company drank 11 unidentified potions to find the healing one. It was the last vial, and the temple has questions. Soup is advised.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, four members of the Brass Kettle Company walked into the Temple of the Harvest Mother in Brindlemoor on Tuesday after drinking eleven unidentified potions in a row, hoping one of them would be a potion of healing. One was. It was the eleventh, and by then the only member of the party who still needed healing was the one who had already had it.

The trouble began on Undermaw Level Three, where the dwarf fighter Dagna Stoneweld broke an ankle on a loose flagstone. The party's satchel held eleven unlabeled vials. Wizard Pim Orchardsby proposed testing them one at a time, and the party agreed to a fair rotation, so that nobody went without a taste. "We didn't want anyone to feel left out of the hurting," Pim told the temple clerk, who wrote it down.

The results, as read from the intake ledger: one potion of diminution, which shrank the ranger to the size of a housecat and left her armor behind in a heap. One potion of climbing, which stuck the bard to the ceiling of the chamber for nine hours. One potion of gaseous form, which took the rogue up the corridor on a draught and has yet to bring him all the way back. Pim could no longer be seen from the left. The tenth vial was plain pond water with a grudge.

Then the eleventh vial, a potion of healing, was drunk by the bard, who was still on the ceiling and unhurt in every particular. He is reported to be in excellent health. Dagna's ankle was no better, and she carried the whole party to the temple on a hireling's cart, which Ansel Pottage of the Fourth Attempt offered to fetch for free, since his own party tried the same trick.

The old herbals say never to taste what you cannot name, and a recent temple study agrees, finding that the most common injury from a mystery tonic is the tonic. This is the second party this week to treat a satchel of unlabeled vials as a buffet. Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 said the guild "has no rule against it, and is reviewing whether that is the problem."

The temple says the party's bill comes to 340 gold, which is less than one vial of healing at the shop on Tanner's Row, and I find that rather rude of the shop. Tip for any delver reading: a potion of healing is red, tastes faintly of honey, and is marked with a cross at the shop. Ask the person who sold it to you. Or pay a cleric three silver to look at it first.

Friends, if you must test your vials, test them on the least necessary party member, and have the wounded one go first. I'd pair this with a thick split-pea soup, and Nyx Spindlecoil tells me there's a scrying charm for naming potions. Go outside, Nyx.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Banshee Call Center Wins Service Award; Teacups Do Not
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: Wailwell Support, a banshee call center in Brindlemoor, won a service award Tuesday. Sterling Vanmoor calls the shattered glass engagement.
item.content:encoded:
Wailwell Support, the banshee call center on Tallow Row in Brindlemoor, won the Merchants' Service Excellence award Tuesday for the third year running. The company employs 60 banshees and fields roughly 4,000 calls a day, and its customers report that an estimated 212 teacups, 40 windowpanes, and one chandelier fail daily during hold music.

Some people see a wall of broken crockery. I see a customer who is fully engaged. Wailwell has reinvented the support call by making it impossible to ignore, and that, friends, is how you disrupt a sleepy industry.

Managing Wailer Ottoline Brass accepted the award in a gown of mourning silk and a pair of wax earplugs the size of walnuts. "Our resolution rate is 97 percent," she said, "because after the first wail, customers stop asking follow-up questions. Many stop asking anything." She declined to say how many callers were still hard of hearing after the quarter. Her staff shouted that number from the back of the hall, which was not helpful.

Complaints are down 80 percent, a figure Wailwell credits to a recent pivot: dissatisfied customers are now offered a free callback, in which the banshee visits their home. At least 31 households have taken the offer. Nobody has taken it twice.

Brindlemoor's clerks are unhappy, naturally. A delegate from the Hearing-Impaired Clerks' Lodge demanded that Wailwell issue earplugs to its callers. I would remind the Lodge that unions are a headwind to scale. When I met Guildmaster Aldous Pennyfarthing at a charity gala last spring, he told me, "Sterling, a silent customer is a lost customer." I think about that every day, usually while wearing earplugs.

Wailwell is now scouting a second site for 120 more banshees and has asked the council for a noise variance that would let its roof sing after dark. The council, which still has not recovered from the lich merger and its skeleton clerks, said only that it would take the request under advisement as soon as it could find a room with unbroken windows.

Investors loved it. Wailwell stock jumped 11 percent on the news, and a rival firm, Murmur & Co., announced it was exploring "a quieter product," which analysts call a mistake. Brakka Stonesweat wrote a column calling the award a crime against ears. Brakka would, though. Brakka has never in her life been on hold with anything but a rock.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • If the customer shatters, the product is working.
  • Always ask your banshee for a testimonial before the first wail.
  • Wax is a business expense. Write it off.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.
